Hearts of Iron 4 constitutes, without exaggeration, the apotheosis of grand strategy gaming devoted to the Second World War. Paradox Interactive has conjured a simulacrum of staggering scope, one that rewards patience with genuine intellectual satisfaction. The provincial cartography demands careful scholarship, as terrain, infrastructure, and logistical arteries conspire to determine the fate of nations. Production, research, and diplomacy interlace in a lattice of consequence, where no decision exists in isolation. Each nation's focus tree bestows upon it a bespoke historical trajectory and strategic soul. To command Germany is to inhabit an entirely different psychological universe than to steward the Soviet Union or navigate American isolationism. Even the diminutive, seemingly inconsequential nations—Luxembourg among them—yield narratives of unexpected richness and gravity. The division designer elevates military planning to the status of a discipline unto itself, a craft demanding both precision and imagination. The bespoke engineering of tanks and aircraft introduces a further stratum of cerebral engagement. The artificial intelligence entrusted to field marshals, alas, occasionally betrays a certain interpretive fallibility. Trade networks and resource allocation are rendered with an admirable, almost forensic verisimilitude. The learning curve, it must be conceded, ascends with unforgiving steepness. The uninitiated may well find themselves cast adrift in a sea of unfamiliar mechanics. The tutorials offer scaffolding, yet fall conspicuously short of cultivating true mastery. The modding community has, through sustained devotion, extended the title's longevity well beyond its native ambitions. Forums and Discord enclaves alike pulse with an enduring, generous vitality. The downloadable content catalog is voluminous, and its cumulative expense is far from trivial. To forgo these expansions is to forfeit substantial strategic nuance and narrative texture. Performance, regrettably, can falter as protracted campaigns accumulate their historical weight. Multiplayer engagements often exact a considerable toll upon one's disposable hours. Visually, the title favors utilitarian clarity over ostentation. Its musical score and ambient soundscape, however, achieve a quietly evocative resonance. No two campaigns ever converge upon identical trajectories. Alternate history unfurls organically, sculpted by the accumulated weight of player agency. The diplomatic architecture, though serviceable, might yet aspire to greater sophistication. Naval and aerial warfare, labyrinthine as they are, ultimately reward the diligent strategist. For the devoted aficionado of the genre, this title constitutes nothing short of an essential rite of passage. The casual player, by contrast, may find the experience more arduous than pleasurable. The prodigious hours it commands from its adherents speak, eloquently, for themselves. In summation, Hearts of Iron 4 merits an unreserved and emphatic recommendation for the serious connoisseur of strategic gaming.

It takes a long time to get the hang of it, and it's a hard one to recommend because it's not quite like anything I've played before.
I'm a history buff and really wanted to understand it and get into it.  I'm glad I did.
No game is perfect but what I appreciate here is the attention to the logic behind how the conflicts start, and what is needed to sustain or survive one.
At least for me, it's an unusual game that plays far deeper with much more attention to detail than anything I'm used to.  I haven't played paradox games before.

It's not quick to get into, it took me over 100hrs to get a grip on what is required to make sure you've got an idea of what each facet of the game is trying to tell you.
How exactly to both build divisions and keep them supplied, what focuses mean and when and why you should get them.  How to plan way ahead with the type of combat you're going to endure and how to really read the terrain within the map and what divisions to design for it.
How navies work, etc.
It's a very deep but ultimately rewarding experience.
It is a time sink unlike any other.
Until now Civilization was as complex as I'd have cared to try, and it is, but this goes layers deeper.
The hype is real, and justified, but only get into it if you're willing to sink hundreds of hours into restarting and learning.
Only get into it if you're patient even if you do know what you're doing, it's a slow game from an action standpoint but there are so many systems to engage with that it can still seem too fast at times.
Worth a shot if you're looking for a game to sink hundreds if not 1000s of hours into.
In that way you'll at least save money not chasing a new computer.  If you love it, it very well could be the last game you play for a very long time.
It was worth the effort and I expect another several hundred hours are in my future.

It'll probably be a few hundred hours before I even consider needing something new.

Hearts of Iron IV, also known as HOI4, is a grand strategy game developed by Paradox Interactive. The game is set during World War II, and players can control almost any country in the world.

Looking back 10 years since launch (and 8 years since I first started playing), it's a genre-defining game that remains relevant for a good reason. I think the hours I've played speak for themselves. The modding possibilities are also almost endless, and the biggest factor that keeps making me revisit this game.

That being said, avoid the latest DLCs like a plague. The base game itself is solid, and much of the content added by recent DLCs is, in my opinion, far inferior to many of the mods you can download on the workshop for free. I even suspect that the devs may be ripping off of existing mods and selling half-baked versions as DLCs. The only DLCs I would recommend, if any, are No Step Back (for the tank designer), Arms Against Tyranny (for the arms market and MIOs), and By Blood Alone (for the plane designer). I myself haven't bought these and only tried them via a previous subscription to get a taste. Everything after these, even Götterdammerung, feels superfluous and unnecessary to enhance the game, and I'd even say that given the poor track record of recent expansions, players should start boycotting new DLCs unless the devs change how they design new content.

Still, overall, the base game is well-developed, and if you want more content, I highly recommend mods. Especially total overhaul ones with far more flavour and depth than what the otherwise-decent base game already has.

Side note: This is an unpopular opinion, but I feel the game's alternate history paths have swerved too far in the direction of wacky implausibility. I'd prefer more grounded paths that actually make sense given the situation in the 1930s, no more resurrecting long-dead kingdoms empires out of the wazoo just for LARP's sake. More in-depth political mechanics would also be very welcome, countries should not be able to switch ideologies and trigger civil wars at a whim, there should be even more build-up than what currently exists.


TLDR: base game good, DLCs (mostly) bad, mods even better

9/10 — I have 88 hours and I still have no idea what I'm doing.

Hearts of Iron IV is one of those games where you start off thinking, "Yeah, I'll play for an hour," and suddenly you've spent your entire night reorganising an army because some random country decided to completely destroy the world order.

I've got around 88 hours so far, and honestly, I'm still learning. The learning curve isn't a curve — it's basically a vertical wall covered in spreadsheets, division templates, supply hubs and buttons that I am still too scared to press.

That being said, HOI4 is insanely fun once things start making sense.

The focus trees are probably one of my favourite parts of the game. Being able to take countries in completely different political and historical directions gives the game a ridiculous amount of replayability. I mostly play ahistorical, which makes everything even better because you genuinely have no idea what's going to happen. You can start a game expecting something somewhat normal and then look over five years later to discover Europe has completely imploded, some minor nation has become a world power and the timeline is beyond saving.

I normally play countries like the USA, Australia, UK, Japan and smaller nations, and every country can feel completely different depending on what path you take.

The warfare and army management is also incredibly satisfying. Building up your military, planning offensives, managing fronts and finally watching your army break through enemy lines after preparing for ages feels amazing.

Then there's the modding community, which is honestly one of the best parts of HOI4. Mods add an absolutely stupid amount of content to the game. I've played Millennium Dawn and The Fire Rises, and they basically feel like entirely different games built inside HOI4. The modding scene alone gives you hundreds, if not thousands, of extra hours of potential gameplay.

However.

The AI has the strategic intelligence of a wet piece of cardboard.

Sometimes your allies will do something so unbelievably stupid that you just have to stare at the screen and accept that whatever plan you had is now dead.

And then there's the naval system.

I don't understand it.

I don't think the navy understands it.

I'm not convinced Paradox understands it.

Naval invasions especially suck ass. Half the time I'm sitting there trying to figure out why my invasion won't launch, only to discover I apparently don't have naval supremacy in some microscopic patch of ocean halfway across the planet.

The performance can also become pretty rough later in the game. Once the entire world has millions of divisions running around, the game starts reconsidering whether time itself should continue moving.

I've also had an annoying issue where the Paradox launcher won't properly launch the game, so I have to go into Steam's launch preferences and set it to skip the launcher just so I can actually play.

Despite all of that, I absolutely recommend HOI4.

It's complicated, confusing, occasionally broken and brutally difficult to learn, but once you start understanding how everything connects, there really isn't much else like it.

You can rewrite history, create completely cursed alternate timelines, take minor nations and turn them into major powers, spend hours perfecting an army, download enormous total-conversion mods and then watch your entire military strategy collapse because the AI decided it wanted to do something incomprehensible.
